transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Owen Li (Redwood CSM); Rajiv Menon (CTO), Lena Ortiz (SRE Lead), Avery Cole (PM), Samir Vega (ML Eng)

Summary: Quick retrospective of week-3 pilot benchmarks vs their existing baseline (CloudX managed endpoints). Reviewed latency/throughput tradeoffs, identified an edge-case with long sequence bursts, discussed quantization/regimen and KV cache hit rates, and agreed next steps to share per-sequence histograms + a dedicated pricing sketch.

Topics: baseline numbers, p50/p95/p99 comparisons, continuous batching impact, cache warmup, model variant fallbacks, VPC/KMS and SOC2 questions, next steps and owners.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, is timing still good on your side?
[00:06] Rajiv: Yeah, all good, thanks. We have about an hour, that's perfect.
[00:10] Jordan: Cool. Maya and I will run through the week three benchmark snapshot we ran overnight against your traffic sample, and then leave time for SRE questions.
[00:18] Lena: Perfect, we've got Samir here to answer any infra specifics.
[00:21] Maya: Quick housekeeping: numbers in the slide are median and percentiles from the 10k reqs you shared, and baseline is the CloudX managed endpoint you told us about. There's some jitter at the tail that we'll point out.
[00:33] Samir: Right, also FYI the production bursts have like 20% of requests over 1k tokens, that might matter.
[00:41] Maya: Exactly, so first chart p50 latency: Redwood hosted with our continuous batching profile hit p50 of 42 ms, baseline was 65 ms. p95 was 128 ms vs 210 ms, and p99: 420 ms vs 890 ms.
[00:56] Avery: Those p99s are... impressive. What's the model variant and quantization there?
[01:03] Maya: We're running the LLaMA-deriv v2 quantized at 4-bit with some kernel-level optimizations; that reduces memory footprint and lets us keep more active contexts in GPU, which helps tail. There's also prefix/KV caching on repeated user prompts which improved effective throughput for short-concat patterns.
[01:21] Rajiv: Hm, our baseline uses CloudX with 8-bit quantization but without the same KV cache and custom kernel selection they don't get the same tail benefits. Could you share how much caching helped?
[01:31] Maya: Sure — in this run cache hit rate averaged 28% across the sample set, and for sessions where hit rate was >50% p99 dropped by ~35%. I'll attach per-session hit breakdown.
[01:41] Lena: Can I ask about burst handling — we saw a big spike on 2025-10-29 in our logs. Your dedicated plan would smooth that out?
[01:50] Jordan: With Dedicated you get a reserved GPU pool and configurable autoscaling policies; plus we can allocate burst capacity for your busiest windows. That trades cost for predictable p99s.
[01:58] Lena: And what about VPC/private? We need KMS and audit logs, can't have keys leaving our VPC.
[02:05] Owen: Yes, for Private deploy we offer customer-managed KMS integrations and audit log streaming to your SIEM. We can show a reference architecture in the next SRE deep dive.
[02:15] Rajiv: Great. One of our worries is the cost delta — CloudX bills per-request, we have tight unit cost targets. How do these batching/caching gains translate to token/unit cost?
[02:26] Maya: In short: caching and dynamic batching reduced tokens-per-infer by ~12% in this sample because repeated contexts avoid regen. From a throughput angle, Redwood hosted achieved ~1,600 effective inferences/sec on the test pool vs baseline 1,050, so cost per effective inference was lower in our setup even with reserved units factored. We'll send a per-model cost breakdown.
[02:47] Samir: How sensitive are those numbers to sequence-length skew? I mean if we start getting a higher fraction of long sequences will your p99 blow up?
[02:55] Maya: Good question. We ran a stress scenario with 30% > 1k token sequences — p99 moved from 420 to around 760 ms on hosted, whereas baseline jumped to 1.5s. We also have quantization+kernel knobs that help but long seqs are expensive, so we recommended a mixed approach: use model variant with sparse attention or segmented chunking for the heaviest tails.
[03:17] Rajiv: That chunking approach — does it alter output fidelity? For clinical notes we can't have hallucinations due to chunking.
[03:25] Maya: We're careful: chunking is used only for scoring/embedding phases or for retrieval-augmented generation where you reassemble with overlap. For generation-critical flows we prefer dedicated capacity and specialized model variants to preserve fidelity. We'll include a fidelity vs throughput table.
[03:40] Avery: Any issues with cold-starts? We saw a 2s cold-start at baseline sometimes.
[03:45] Maya: Cold-starts are mostly eliminated on Dedicated because we keep warm pools and liveness probes; hosted had a small cold window for infrequent model loads but our warm cache policy keeps active models resident based on recent traffic.
[03:56] Lena: Security/regulatory: SOC2 scope — do you have the attestation and can we get the controls mapping?
[04:03] Owen: We are SOC 2 Type II and maintain a controls mapping doc for common requests; we'll share that plus a redacted pen test summary. KMS integration and SAML/SSO are standard for Private.
[04:13] Rajiv: Good. Also latency SLA — can you hit p99 < 800 ms for our heavy hours under Dedicated?
[04:19] Jordan: Based on current numbers and expected traffic, Dedicated with the recommended CPU/GPU ratio and burst policy gives you room to meet that 800 ms p99 target; we'll produce a capacity plan and run a targeted load test to validate.
[04:30] Samir: For the load test, can we use our production-like traffic generator? We want realistic token distributions.
[04:35] Maya: Absolutely — in fact please send your seq-length histogram and we will replay it in our test harness.
[04:40] Rajiv: We'll do that. One quick nit — the baseline includes a multi-tenant busiest host which we think is causing some of their tail. Your dedicated numbers are comparing to their multi-tenant median; is that apples-to-apples?
[04:50] Maya: We attempted to match request patterns and cold-start frequency; but you're right the baseline environment is multi-tenant and sometimes suffers noisy neighbors. Our replication note will call that out explicitly.
[04:58] Lena: Can you also share the raw CSVs for the latency percentiles and per-request sequence length? Our SRE wants to do independent analysis.
[05:05] Jordan: Yes, action item: Maya will export histograms and raw CSV and drop into the shared drive.
[05:11] Owen: Another note for procurement — pricing for Dedicated vs hosted: Jordan will sketch reserved commit tiers and an example run rate.
[05:17] Jordan: I'll do that. Also, I'll include expected cost-per-1M-infers for the two configurations.
[05:22] Avery: For rollout, we want canary behavior in the first two weeks and an automatic fallback to baseline if p99 go above threshold. Do you support that?
[05:30] Maya: Yes, our rollout system supports traffic mirroring, canaries by percentage, and automatic fallback to a configured alternate endpoint. We'll send a sample rollout policy you can copy.
[05:38] Rajiv: Any blockers on compliance for us?
[05:41] Owen: None on our end beyond signing a DPA and agreeing network controls for Private. We'll prepare the DPA draft after the SRE deep-dive.
[05:47] Lena: Sounds good.
[05:49] Jordan: Okay to recap — send raw CSV & histograms, send dedicated pricing sketch, schedule SRE deep-dive for VPC/KMS, and Rajiv team will provide seq-length distribution. Anything else?
[06:02] Avery: Please add a sample canary rollback policy and a short note on fidelity testing for chunked flows.
[06:09] Jordan: Noted. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up and get those artifacts out by the dates we discussed.
[06:13] Rajiv: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
